author: "Elisabetta Canteri"

# Abstract {-}

Describing and interpreting cultural history and transmission has been a central focus of archaeology for over a century. New information coming from ancient DNA has revealed the fundamental role of demography in shaping both genomic and cultural change. Yet, the effects of demographic processes on the spatial and temporal distributions of cultural and genomic patterns are still poorly understood. Here, we examine the relations between demography and space-time patterns of genomic variation and cultural traditions, by testing whether shifts in genomic patterns correspond to spatiotemporal changes in burial rites. Our approach uses data accessed from the Big Interdisciplinary Archaeological Database (BIAD), linking mortuary information from approximately 4,200 individuals with genetic ancestry and mobility data inferred from over 1,300 human genomes, spanning vast parts of Western Eurasia over the last 10,000 years. By integrating and modeling these diverse datasets, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of how human mobility and demographic change intersect with cultural traditions, offering new insights into the dynamics behind culture history, and the extent to which genes and culture are transmitted in parallel.

# Aim {-}

This book will show all the main results of the project. We start by exploring the data on burial rites and their link with genetically-derived measures of human ancestry and mobility.

# Burial data

Here we are going to track the analysis on the data that Robert and Stephen shared with us. 

We want to explore whether we can find a relationship between large scale human migrations and changes in burial practices during he Holocene.

We will analyse burial practices data against a Gaussian spatial process and values of human ancestry and mobility. The data we have are records of different burial types at grave sites across Europe.

Let's first input the data. We are going to transform characters to factors for the explanatory variables we need, so we can check how many levels they have. 

## Data table

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# graves <- fread("./EAA2024_burial_rite_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = F, na.strings = "\\N")
graves <- fread("./Data/Burial.csv", na.strings = "")
graves$DepositionType <- as.factor(graves$DepositionType)
graves$BodyPositioning <- as.factor(graves$BodyPositioning)
graves$BurialSide <- as.factor(graves$BurialSide)
str(graves)
```

As we can see, some of the variables we are most interested in, such as the positioning of the body and the burial side, have more than 2 levels. This means that there are more than 2 descriptors for each variable. This makes it tricky because we cannot model factors with more that 2 levels. Therefore, we will create new columns in the database where we transform the factors to a binomial presence/absence data (0/1).

```{r, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
factor_to_binomial <- function(d){
  require(pbapply)
  cols <- which(sapply(d, is.factor))
  l <- sapply(d[, ..cols], levels)
  new_col_names <- lapply(1:length(l), function(x) sapply(l[[x]], function(n) paste0(names(l)[x], "_", n)))
  pblapply(1:length(new_col_names), function(f){
    sapply(1:length(new_col_names[[f]]), function(x){
      c <- names(l)[f]
      bin <- sapply(d[, ..c], function(b) ifelse(b == l[[f]][x], 1, 0))
      d[, new_col_names[[f]][x] := bin]
      return(d)
    })
    return(d)
  })
  return(d)
}

factor_to_binomial(graves)
str(graves)
fwrite(graves, "./Burial.csv")
```

Also, for the Burial Side variable, we have a level called "left?" in the original data table, what should we do with this? Can we group this with the left or not? For now I grouped it because it consists of just 5 records, but we can decide later whether we should keep it separate or not.

```{r, echo = F, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
graves[BurialSide == "left?"]$BurialSide <- "left"
graves$BurialSide <- droplevels(factor(graves$BurialSide)[factor(graves$BurialSide) != "left?"])
```

The burial orientation seems interesting because the majority of the data lies on specific angles, for example: 0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, and 270.

The body positioning also seems to aggregate towards "crouched", "inside a vessel", "extended", and "scattered", with the two most represented groups being "crouched" and "inside a vessel".

## Adding ancestry and mobility

The next step is to pair the grave individuals with human ancestry and mobility data. For some of them, the aDNAID will match, so we have confidence that the values assigned to those graves are correct. For others, we might have to take values of ancestry and mobility of the closest individuals in space and time.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## Ancestry
ancestry <- fread("../MesoNeo/MesoNeo/Data3/combined.tsv")
info <- fread("/Users/msb290/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofCopenhagen/MesoNeo/MesoNeo/Data3/neo.impute.1000g.sampleInfo_clusterInfo.txt")
ancestry2 <- melt(ancestry, id.vars = 1:4, measure.vars = 5:13, variable.name = "ANCE")
ancestry2 <- merge(ancestry2, info[, .(sampleId, country, region, groupLabel, clusterAlias)], by.x = "IND", by.y = "sampleId")
ggplot(data = ancestry2, aes(x = forcats::fct_reorder(IND, TIME, .desc = T), y = value, color = ANCE, fill = ANCE)) +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') + 
  scale_color_manual(values = pals::coolwarm(9)) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = pals::coolwarm(9)) + 
  facet_wrap(~region, scales = "free") + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), 
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid = element_blank())

## Mobility
ov <- fread("~/Documents/Postdoc/mobest/tables/Dataset_S3.csv")
ov2 <- fread("~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofCopenhagen/mobest/tables/mobility_estimates_250y_retrospecive_distance.csv")
info <- fread("~/Documents/Postdoc/mobest/tables/Dataset_S1.csv")
mobility <- merge(ov2, info, by = "Sample_ID", all.x = T)
rm(ov, ov2, info)
# remove modern individuals
ancestry <- ancestry[TIME > 0]
# transform time of mobility data from BC/AD to cal BP
mobility[, Date_BP_Start := 1950 - Date_BC_AD_Start]
mobility[, Date_BP_Median := 1950 - Date_BC_AD_Median]
mobility[, Date_BP_Stop := 1950 - Date_BC_AD_Stop]

# Number of common IDs
length(which(graves$aDNAID %in% ancestry$IND)) # 3%
length(which(graves$aDNAID %in% mobility$Sample_ID)) # 11%
```

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Merge together
graves <- merge(graves, ancestry[, .(IND, TIME, ANCE1, ANCE2, ANCE3, ANCE4, ANCE5, ANCE6, ANCE7, ANCE8, ANCE9)], by.x = "aDNAID", by.y = "IND", all.x = T)
graves <- merge(graves, mobility[, .(Sample_ID, ov_dist_mds2_retro_default, ov_dist_pca5_retro_default, Date_BP_Median)], by.x = "aDNAID", by.y = "Sample_ID", all.x = T)

# Reconcile ages BP
graves[, YearBP := gaussianModelMu]
graves[!is.na(TIME)]$YearBP <- graves[!is.na(TIME)]$TIME
graves[!is.na(Date_BP_Median)]$YearBP <- graves[!is.na(Date_BP_Median)]$Date_BP_Median
```

We have matched the common IDs, now we try and find the closest individuals to assign the values, starting with mobility estimates.

To match the sites, we will calculate the distances between individuals both in space and in time. We will then add the distances together to calculate values of distances in time and space. We will then extract the individuals with the minimum spatiotemporal distance. We have one problem: for `r length(which(is.na(graves$YearBP)))` graves we do not have an age and therefore we cannot calculate a spatiotemporal distance. I would be cautious of assigning values of mobility and ancestry only based on spatial distance, so I will remove them.

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
graves[, Num := 1:.N]

# Subset data to individuals with no estimates of mobility
miss <- graves[is.na(ov_dist_mds2_retro_default)]

# Remove individuals for which we do not have an age
miss <- miss[!is.na(YearBP)]

# Transform to points under equal-area projection
gr_pnts <- project(
    vect(x = miss[, .(Longitude, Latitude, ov_dist_mds2_retro_default, aDNAID)],
                 geom = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = crs(rast())), 
    proj
  )
mob_pnts <- project(
  vect(mobility[, .(Longitude, Latitude, Sample_ID)], 
         geom = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
         crs = crs(rast())), 
  proj
)
```

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
conts_prj <- st_transform(conts, crs = proj)
e <- c(min(c(ext(mob_pnts)[1], ext(gr_pnts)[1])),
       max(c(ext(mob_pnts)[2], ext(gr_pnts)[2])),
       min(c(ext(mob_pnts)[3], ext(gr_pnts)[3])),
       max(c(ext(mob_pnts)[4], ext(gr_pnts)[4])))
plot(mob_pnts, col = "red", xlim = e[1:2], ylim = e[3:4]); points(gr_pnts, col = "blue"); plot(conts_prj$geometry, add = T)
```

Here we get the closest individual in spatiotemporal distance.
```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Calculate euclidean distance in space
spatdists <- distance(gr_pnts, mob_pnts, unit = "km")

# Calculate euclidean distance in time
pairs <- expand.grid(miss$YearBP, mobility$Date_BP_Median)
tempdists <- apply(pairs, 1, function(r) sqrt(sum((r[1] - r[2])^2)))
tempdists <- matrix(tempdists, 
                    nrow = length(miss$YearBP), 
                    ncol = length(mobility$Date_BP_Median))

# spatiotemporal distances (euclidean with km == year)
st_dists <- sqrt((spatdists + tempdists)^2)

# Find minimum spatial distance
find_min <- function(row) {
  which(row == min(row))
}
min_columns <- apply(st_dists, 1, find_min)
min_dists <- apply(st_dists, 1, min)

# Get Sample_ID in mobility table
ids <- lapply(min_columns, function(x) mobility$Sample_ID[x])
```

```{r}
gr_pnts <- project(
  vect(graves[, .(Longitude, Latitude, aDNAID, Num)], geom = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), 
                crs = crs(rast())),
  proj)
ance_pnts <- project(
  vect(ancestry[, .(LON, LAT, IND)], 
                 geom = c("LON", "LAT"),
                 crs = crs(rast())),
  proj)
mob_pnts <- project(
  vect(mobility[, .(Longitude, Latitude, Sample_ID)], 
                 geom = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
                 crs = crs(rast())),
  proj)

e <- c(min(c(ext(mob_pnts)[1], ext(gr_pnts)[1]), ext(ance_pnts)[1]),
       max(c(ext(mob_pnts)[2], ext(gr_pnts)[2]), ext(ance_pnts)[2]),
       min(c(ext(mob_pnts)[3], ext(gr_pnts)[3]), ext(ance_pnts)[3]),
       max(c(ext(mob_pnts)[4], ext(gr_pnts)[4]), ext(ance_pnts)[4]))
conts_prj <- st_transform(conts, crs = proj)
plot(conts_prj$geometry, xlim = e[1:2], ylim = e[3:4]); points(ance_pnts, bg = "skyblue", pch = 21, cex = 1.5); points(mob_pnts, bg = alpha("violet", 0.5), pch = 22, cex = 1); points(gr_pnts, bg = alpha("gold", 0.8), pch = 24, cex = 1)
```

We have now the matching IDs with the minimum spatiotemporal distances between the grave individuals and the mobility estimates. In some instances, we have more than 1 match. In this case, I will take the average mobility estimate across the matched ones. 

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Extract human mobility value
# MDS based
ov_mds <- pblapply(ids, function(x){
  d <- mobility[Sample_ID %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(mean(d$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default, na.rm = T))
  } else {
    return(d$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default)
  }
})
ov_mds <- lapply(ov_mds, function(x) ifelse(length(x) > 0, x, NA))

# PCA based
ov_pca <- pblapply(ids, function(x){
  d <- mobility[Sample_ID %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(mean(d$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default, na.rm = T))
  } else {
    return(d$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default)
  }
})
ov_pca <- lapply(ov_pca, function(x) ifelse(length(x) > 0, x, NA))
```

We need to acknowledge that in some cases the spatiotemporal distance could be very wide, which could create some bias during the analysis. This results from individuals that have no close match in space or time, or in spacetime, leading to choose the least distant. Here we can see a plot of the distribution of the calculated spatiotemporal distances:

### Radius approach

Here we extract 3-4 closest individuals within a 350 km radius and up to 300 years apart. If there is only 1 individual, I take the value for that one. If there are two, I take the average mobility value for those two, same for up to 4 individuals.

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
d <- apply(spatdists, 1, function(x) which(x <= 350))
t <- apply(tempdists, 1, function(x) which(x <= 300))

prod <- lapply(1:length(d), function(x) which(d[[x]] %in% t[[x]])) # match between spat and temp
prod_idx <- lapply(1:length(prod), function(x) d[[x]][prod[[x]]]) # get index
# Sort distances to get the smallest within the 400 km+yrs spatiotemporal radius
dists <- lapply(1:length(prod_idx), function(i) {
  v <- st_dists[i, prod_idx[[i]]]
  names(v) <- prod_idx[[i]]
  return(sort(v))
  })

mob_ids <- lapply(1:length(dists), function(x){
  if(length(dists[[x]]) >= 1){
    ix <- as.numeric(names(dists[[x]]))[1:4]
    ix <- ix[!is.na(ix)]
    return(mobility$Sample_ID[ix])
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
})

## Extract mobility values
# MDS
mds_dist <- pbsapply(mob_ids, function(x){
  d <- mobility[Sample_ID %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(mean(d$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default, na.rm = T))
  } else if(nrow(d) == 1){
    return(d$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default)
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
})

# PCA
pca_dist <- pbsapply(mob_ids, function(x){
  d <- mobility[Sample_ID %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(mean(d$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default, na.rm = T))
  } else if(nrow(d) == 1){
    return(d$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default)
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
})

## Add to table
miss$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default <- ov_mds
miss$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default <- ov_pca
miss$mobility_MDS_method2 <- mds_dist
miss$mobility_PCA_method2 <- pca_dist

## Fill gaps in graves table
graves[, MobilityMatch_distance := as.numeric(NA)]
graves[Num %in% miss$Num]$MobilityMatch_distance <- min_dists
graves[Num %in% miss$Num]$ov_dist_mds2_retro_default <- unlist(ov_mds)
graves[Num %in% miss$Num]$ov_dist_pca5_retro_default <- unlist(ov_pca)
graves[, mobility_MDS_method2 := as.numeric(NA)]
graves[, mobility_PCA_method2 := as.numeric(NA)]
graves[miss$Num,]$mobility_MDS_method2 <- miss$mobility_MDS_method2
graves[miss$Num,]$mobility_PCA_method2 <- miss$mobility_PCA_method2
```

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
summary(graves$MobilityMatch_distance)
hist(graves$MobilityMatch_distance, breaks = 100, main = "Spatiotemporal distance between grave and mobility individuals", xlab = "Distance")

# How many individuals with distance > 500
length(which(graves$MobilityMatch_distance > 500))

# How many individuals with distance > 5000
length(which(graves$MobilityMatch_distance > 5000))
```

We have one individual that has a very large spatiotemporal distance. This is due to the age of the grave (YearBP = `r graves[MobilityMatch_distance > 5000]$YearBP`), being very old. The oldest age of the individuals with mobility estimates is `r max(mobility$Date_BP_Median)`. This creates a combined spatiotemporal distance that is very large. We can discuss whether it would be a good idea to **discard** this grave.

At least, we have few individuals that show very big spatiotemporal distances. We can maybe decide later on if we should put a distance threshold.

Now we do the same for ancestry values.
```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Subset data to individuals with no estimates of ancestry
miss <- graves[is.na(ANCE1)]
# Remove individuals for which we do not have an age
miss <- miss[!is.na(YearBP)]

# Transform to points
gr_pnts <- project(vect(x = miss[, .(Longitude, Latitude, aDNAID, Num, YearBP)],
                        geom = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = crs(rast())),
                   proj)
ance_pnts <- project(vect(ancestry[, .(LON, LAT, IND, TIME)], 
                          geom = c("LON", "LAT"),
                          crs = crs(rast())),
                     proj)
```

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot(ance_pnts, col = "red"); points(gr_pnts, col = "blue"); plot(conts_prj, add = T)
```

We are going to do the same as before.

```{r, eval = F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
## Method 1: minimum spatiotemporal distance
# Calculate euclidean distance in space
spatdists <- distance(gr_pnts, ance_pnts, unit = "km")

# Calculate euclidean distance in time
pairs <- expand.grid(gr_pnts$YearBP, ance_pnts$TIME)
tempdists <- apply(pairs, 1, function(r) sqrt(sum((r[1] - r[2])^2)))
tempdists <- matrix(tempdists, 
                    nrow = length(gr_pnts$YearBP), 
                    ncol = length(ance_pnts$TIME))

# spatiotemporal distances (euclidean with km == year)
st_dists <- sqrt((spatdists + tempdists)^2)

# Find minimum spatial distance
min_columns <- apply(st_dists, 1, find_min)
min_dists <- apply(st_dists, 1, min)

# Get individual ID from ancestry table
ids <- lapply(min_columns, function(x) ancestry$IND[x])

# Extract ancestry value
ance <- paste0("ANCE", 1:9)
anc_vals <- rbindlist(pblapply(ids, function(x){
  d <- ancestry[IND %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(as.data.table(matrix(colMeans(d[, ..ance], na.rm = T), nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, ance))))
  } else {
    return(d[, ..ance])
  }
}))

## Method 2: average across the 4 closest individuals within a 350 km and 300 years radius. This threshold has been chosen to minimize the loss of data (only 16% now are not paired with an ancestry value)
d <- apply(spatdists, 1, function(x) which(x <= 350))
t <- apply(tempdists, 1, function(x) which(x <= 300))

prod <- lapply(1:length(d), function(x) which(d[[x]] %in% t[[x]])) # match between spat and temp
prod_idx <- lapply(1:length(prod), function(x) d[[x]][prod[[x]]]) # get index
# Sort distances to get the smallest within the spatiotemporal radius
dists <- lapply(1:length(prod_idx), function(i) {
  v <- st_dists[i, prod_idx[[i]]]
  names(v) <- prod_idx[[i]]
  return(sort(v))
  })

ance_ids <- lapply(1:length(dists), function(x){
  if(length(dists[[x]]) >= 1){
    ix <- as.numeric(names(dists[[x]]))[1:4]
    ix <- ix[!is.na(ix)]
    return(ancestry$IND[ix])
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
})

## Extract ancestry values
ance_lookup <- ancestry[, .(IND, ANCE1, ANCE2, ANCE3, ANCE4, ANCE5, ANCE6, ANCE7, ANCE8, ANCE9)]
ance_v2 <- rbindlist(pblapply(ance_ids, function(x){
  d <- ance_lookup[IND %in% x]
  if(nrow(d) > 1){
    return(as.data.table(matrix(colMeans(d[, ..ance], na.rm = T), nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, ance))))
  } else if(nrow(d) == 1){
    return(d[, ..ance])
  } else {
    return(data.table(ANCE1 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE2 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE3 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE4 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE5 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE6 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE7 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE8 = as.numeric(NA), 
                      ANCE9 = as.numeric(NA)))
  }
}))
length(which(is.na(ance_v2$ANCE1)))/nrow(ance_v2) # 16% NAs

# Create table of ancestry values
anc_vals[, Num := miss$Num]
names(ance_v2) <- paste0(names(ance_v2), "_v2")
ance_v2[, Num := miss$Num]

# Add minimum distance between grave individuals and ancestry individuals
graves[, AncestryMatch_distance := as.numeric(NA)]
graves[miss$Num,]$AncestryMatch_distance <- min_dists

# Fill the gaps
for(a in ance){
  graves[anc_vals$Num, a] <- anc_vals[, ..a]
}
graves[, names(ance_v2)[-length(names(ance_v2))] := as.numeric(NA)]
graves[ance_v2$Num, names(ance_v2)[-length(names(ance_v2))]] <- ance_v2[, .(ANCE1_v2, ANCE2_v2, ANCE3_v2, ANCE4_v2, ANCE5_v2, ANCE6_v2, ANCE7_v2, ANCE8_v2, ANCE9_v2)]
```

```{r}
summary(graves$AncestryMatch_distance)
hist(graves$AncestryMatch_distance, breaks = 100, main = "Spatiotemporal distance between graves and ancestry", xlab = "Distance")

length(which(graves$AncestryMatch_distance > 500))
length(which(graves$AncestryMatch_distance > 5000))
```

We have now all the data ready to be analysed, but we still need to set up the inlabru model.

# Burial rites
## Data
```{r data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results = "hide"}
# graves <- fread("./EAA2024_burial_rite_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = F, na.strings = "\\N")
graves <- fread("./Data/Burial.csv", na.strings = "")
graves$DepositionType <- as.factor(graves$DepositionType)
graves$BodyPositioning <- as.factor(graves$BodyPositioning)
graves$BurialSide <- as.factor(graves$BurialSide)

# Sites table (BIAD)
sites <- setDT(query.database("SELECT * FROM `Sites`", conn))

# Culture and Period
culture <- fread("./Data/burial rites_culture_period.csv", na.strings = "\\N")
culture <- culture[!duplicated(IndividualID)]

## Add info to graves table
graves <- merge(graves, sites[, .(SiteID, Country)], by = "SiteID", all.x = T)
rm(sites)
graves <- merge(graves, culture, by = "IndividualID", all.x = T)

## Remove outlier
graves <- graves[!is.na(YearBP)]
graves <- graves[YearBP < 15000]
summary(graves$YearBP)
```

## Multiple correspondence analysis
```{r mca, warning=F, message=F, fig.dpi=300}
## Data
bp <- grep("BodyPositioning_", colnames(graves))
bs <- grep("BurialSide_", colnames(graves))
mat <- as.data.frame(cbind(graves[, ..bp], graves[, ..bs]))
mat <- as.matrix(mat)
dim(mat)

## Multiple Correspondence Analysis
mca <- MCA(graves[, .(BurialSide, BodyPositioning)], graph = F)
summary(mca)

## Biplot
# Dimensions 1 and 2
fviz_mca_biplot(mca,
                col.ind = c("#C1E8AF"),
                col.var = c("#382F55"),
                alpha.ind = 0.2,
                repel = FALSE, # Avoid text overlapping (slow if many point)
                ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)
knitr::include_graphics("~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofCopenhagen/Graves/Figures/MCA_biplot.png")

# Dimensions 1 and 3
fviz_mca_biplot(mca,
                axes = c(1,3),
                col.ind = c("#C1E8AF"),
                col.var = c("#382F55"),
                alpha.ind = 0.2,
                repel = FALSE, # Avoid text overlapping (slow if many point)
                ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)

## Eigenvalues
eig.val <- get_eigenvalue(mca)
fviz_screeplot(mca)

## Look at the quality of representation of variable categories
fviz_cos2(mca, choice = "var", axes = 1:2)
fviz_cos2(mca, choice = "var", axes = c(1,3))

## Extract results for individuals
ind <- get_mca_ind(mca)
# Coordinates of points
head(ind$coord)
# Quality of representation
head(ind$cos2)
# Contributions
head(ind$contrib)

## Extract results for variables
var <- get_mca_var(mca)
# Coordinates of points
head(var$coord)
# Quality of representation
head(var$cos2)
# Contributions
head(var$contrib)

## Dimension description
res.desc <- dimdesc(mca, axes = c(1,2,3))
# Description of dimension 1
res.desc[[1]]
# Description of dimension 2
res.desc[[2]]
# Description of dimension 3
res.desc[[3]]
```

## UpSet plot
We can produce an UpSet plot to better visualize the structure of the data. An UpSet plot is a simplified visualization of a Venn diagram.

```{r UpSet plot, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
upset_df <- graves[, .(IndividualID, BodyPositioning_crouched, BodyPositioning_extended, `BodyPositioning_extended, rhomboid`, BodyPositioning_heap, `BodyPositioning_inside a vessel`, BodyPositioning_irregular, BodyPositioning_prone, BodyPositioning_scattered, BodyPositioning_sitting, BurialSide_back, `BurialSide_back/left`, `BurialSide_back/right`, BurialSide_bottom, BurialSide_front, `BurialSide_front/left`, `BurialSide_front/right`, BurialSide_left, `BurialSide_left/back`, `BurialSide_left/front`, BurialSide_right, `BurialSide_right/back`, `BurialSide_right/front`)]

# UpSet plot with all variables
upset(upset_df, sets = colnames(upset_df)[-1], order.by = 'freq', keep.order = F)
set_size <- data.frame(Set = colnames(upset_df)[-1],
                       Size = colSums(upset_df[,-1], na.rm = T))
ggplot(data = set_size) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = reorder(Set, Size, decreasing = T), y = Size), stat = "identity") +
  theme_bw() +
  ylab("Set Size") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 10, l = 30, b = 5))

# UpSet plot with selected variables
sets <- c("BodyPositioning_crouched", "BodyPositioning_extended", "BodyPositioning_heap", "BodyPositioning_inside a vessel", "BodyPositioning_prone", "BodyPositioning_scattered", "BodyPositioning_sitting","BurialSide_bottom", "BurialSide_front", "BurialSide_left", "BurialSide_right", "BurialSide_back")
upset(upset_df, sets = sets, order.by = 'freq', keep.order = T, set_size.show = T)

set_size <- set_size[which(set_size$Set %in% sets),]
ggplot(data = set_size) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = reorder(Set, Size, decreasing = T), y = Size), stat = "identity") +
  theme_bw() +
  ylab("Set Size") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 5, r = 10, l = 20, b = 5))

```

Now let's plot the MCA biplots without the repel option. We color the individuals by other variables, including **culture**, **period**, **country**, and **ancestry** values.

In this case, because the individuals are too many, I decided to count the number of individuals in each variable and for each dimension coordinate.

```{r biplots, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ind_dims$WHG <- graves$ANCE4_v2
ind_dims$LVN <- graves$ANCE6_v2
```

```{r culture, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.dim=c(14,10)}
culture_keep <- ind_dims[!is.na(Culture)][, .N, by = "Culture"][order(N, decreasing = T)][, Culture][1:10]

# png("../Figures/Biplot_Culture.png", width = 14, height = 10, units = 'in', res = 330)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dim_culture[Culture %in% culture_keep],
             aes(x = `Dim 1`, y = `Dim 2`,
                 fill = Culture,
                 size = N),
             position = position_jitter(0.2, 0.2),
             shape = 21) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pals::tol.rainbow(10),
                    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))) +
  scale_size_continuous("Count", breaks = c(1,25,50,100,150, 200),
                        range = c(3, 20)) +
  geom_point(data = var_dims,
             aes(x = `Dim 1`, y = `Dim 2`),
             shape = 23,
             fill = 'white',
             alpha = 0.5,
             size = 3,
             stroke = 1) +
  geom_label_repel(data = var_dims,
                   aes(x = `Dim 1`, y = `Dim 2`, label = Variable),
                   segment.color = 'black',
                   segment.alpha = 0.5,
                   fill = alpha("white", 0.8),
                   max.overlaps = 50,
                   nudge_x = 1,
                   nudge_y = 0.5,
                   direction = "both") +
  xlab(paste0("Dim 1 (", round(eig.val[1,2], 2), "%)")) +
  ylab(paste0("Dim 2 (", round(eig.val[2,2], 2), "%)")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.box = "vertical",
        legend.direction = "vertical")
# dev.off()
```

## Modelling

We decided, based on the upset plot, to model the burial sides: *right*, *left*, *back* against ancestry and mobility. This is because both left and right are associated with the crouched position and the back is associated with the extended position, which are the most commonly found positions in graves.

### Model fit

Here we take a look at the model fit. We tested different models, with different combinations of covariates. Her we take a look at the model fit, based on WAIC and DIC scores.

```{r model fit, fig.dim = c(10,15), echo = F}
model_info <- data.frame(
    model = paste0("m", 1:10),
    name = c(
        "baseline",
        "baseline + mobility + ancestry",
        "baseline + ancestry",
        "baseline + no WHG ancestry",
        "baseline + no WHG ancestry + mobility",
        "baseline + EHG",
        "baseline + WHG",
        "baseline + CHG",
        "baseline + LVN",
        "baseline + mobility"
    )
)

model_5k_info <- data.frame(
    model = paste0("mb", 1:3),
    name = c(
        "baseline",
        "baseline + no WHG ancestry",
        "baseline + no WHG ancestry + mobility"
    )
)

model_steppe_info <- data.frame(
    model = paste0("ms", 1:4),
    name = c(
        "baseline",
        "baseline + mobility + steppe ancestry + LVN",
        "baseline + steppe ancestry + LVN",
        "baseline + steppe ancestry"
    )
)

# Model fit
model_fit <- fread("./Results/Models_fit.csv")
model_5k_fit <- fread("./Results/ModelsFit_BeforeSteppe.csv")
model_steppe_fit <- fread("./Results/ModelsFit_Steppe.csv")

## Plot model fit
# Whole period
model_fit$Model <- factor(model_fit$Model, levels = unique(model_fit$Model))
model_fit[, deltaWAIC := waic - min(waic), by = "Variable"]
model_fit[, colorWAIC := ifelse(deltaWAIC == 0, "red", "black")]
model_fit[, deltaDIC := dic - min(dic), by = "Variable"]
model_fit[, colorDIC := ifelse(deltaDIC == 0, "red", "black")]
model_fit$Variable <- factor(model_fit$Variable, levels = unique(model_fit$Variable))

p1 <- ggplot(data = model_fit) +
    geom_line(aes(x = Model, y = deltaWAIC, group = 1)) +
    geom_hline(
        data = model_fit[Model == "baseline"], aes(yintercept = deltaWAIC),
        linetype = 2, color = "black"
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(x = Model, y = deltaWAIC, fill = colorWAIC), shape = 21, size = 4) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(Variable), scales = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    ylab("Delta WAIC") +
    ggtitle("Whole period") +
    labs(tag = "A") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20, hjust = 0.5),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16),
        aspect.ratio = 0.2,
        plot.tag = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 22)
    )

p2 <- ggplot(data = model_fit) +
    geom_line(aes(x = Model, y = deltaDIC, group = 1)) +
    geom_hline(
        data = model_fit[Model == "baseline"], aes(yintercept = deltaDIC),
        linetype = 2, color = "black"
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(x = Model, y = deltaDIC, fill = colorDIC), shape = 21, size = 4) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(Variable), scales = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    ylab("Delta DIC") +
    labs(tag = "B") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        strip.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 16),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 16),
        aspect.ratio = 0.2,
        plot.tag = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 22)
    )
library(patchwork)
p1/p2
```

### Calculating the average

Now that we have imported the data, we need to calculate the mean angle for each individual. We have the min and max, but we will work with the mean. There are cases where the min angle is the only angle available. In that case, the min will be used as the mean.

We have two ways to get the mean angles:

1.  Use a custom function that we create

2.  Use the `mean.circular` function of the `circular` package.

We can compare the two to see how they perform.

```{r b-o mean function}
## We can't just average between the min and max angles because for some angles the average will be 0, so we will not get burials facing south.
## We create a function to transform the angles that works around this issue.
#----------------------------------------------------------------------
find.mid.deg <- function(min.deg, max.deg){
  
  difference <- max.deg - min.deg
  i.accute <- difference<180
  i.obtuse <- difference>180
  i.bad <- difference==180
  
  mid <- numeric()
  mid[i.accute] <- max.deg[i.accute] - difference[i.accute]/2
  mid[i.obtuse] <- max.deg[i.obtuse] + (360 - difference[i.obtuse])/2
  mid[i.bad] <- NA
  
  i <- mid>=360
  mid[i] <- mid[i]-360
  
  i <- mid<0
  mid[i] <- mid[i]+360           
  return(mid)}
#----------------------------------------------------------------------
min.deg <- c(5,15,170,270)
max.deg <- c(356,300,185,360)
find.mid.deg(min.deg, max.deg)
#----------------------------------------------------------------------
```

```{r b-o orientation data}
# Remove NAs in both min and max orientation columns
orientation <- orientation[!(is.na(BurialOrientationMin) & is.na(BurialOrientationMax))]

# Create a table for records that have a single angle value (in BurialOrientationMin)
single_angles <- orientation[is.na(BurialOrientationMax)]
single_angles[, BurialOrientationMean := BurialOrientationMin]

# Remove from overall table
orientation <- orientation[!(is.na(BurialOrientationMin) | is.na(BurialOrientationMax))]

# Average across min and max 
## Using Adrian's function
orientation[, BurialOrientationMean := find.mid.deg(BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax)]

## Using circular package
means <- round(sapply(1:nrow(orientation), function(x) mean.circular(circular(c(orientation$BurialOrientationMin[x], orientation$BurialOrientationMax[x]), type = "angles", units = "degrees", rotation = "clock"))),2)
means <- sapply(1:length(means), function(x) ifelse(means[x] < 0, 360 + means[x], means[x]))

## Check differences
orientation$BurialOrientationMin[698]; orientation$BurialOrientationMax[698]
orientation$BurialOrientationMean[698]; means[698]
```

In this last example we can see that the custom function we have does not recognize 270 as the minimum angle, but it takes 0 as the minimum making the mean **135**. However, because 0 is 360, if we consider 270 as the minimum, the mean should be **315**, as determined by the circular package. 

I believe this is the correct way to move forward, so I will use the mean.circular function to calculate the means.

```{r b-o final data}
orientation[, BurialOrientationMean := means]
# Bind tables together
orientation <- rbind(orientation, single_angles)
orientation <- orientation[order(Num)]

# Calculate cosine and sine from radians
orientation[, BurialOrientationMean_cos := cos(BurialOrientationMean*pi/180)]
orientation[, BurialOrientationMin_cos := cos(BurialOrientationMin*pi/180)]
orientation[, BurialOrientationMax_cos := cos(BurialOrientationMax*pi/180)]
orientation[, BurialOrientationMean_sin := sin(BurialOrientationMean*pi/180)]
orientation[, BurialOrientationMin_sin := sin(BurialOrientationMin*pi/180)]
orientation[, BurialOrientationMax_sin := sin(BurialOrientationMax*pi/180)]

# Add Country, Culture, Period and Ancestry info
orientation$Longitude <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Longitude
orientation$Latitude <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Latitude
orientation$Country <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Country
orientation$Period <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Period
orientation$Culture <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Culture
orientation$Sex <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$Sex
orientation$Age <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$gaussianModelMu
orientation$EHG <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$ANCE2_v2
orientation$WHG <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$ANCE4_v2
orientation$LVN <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$ANCE6_v2
orientation$CHG <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$ANCE8_v2
orientation$mobility <- graves[Num %in% orientation$Num]$mobility_MDS_250y_retrospective

# orientation <- fread("./Data/BurialOrientation.csv", na.strings = "")
```

For the circular histograms, we have to manually create some adjustments in order for ggplot to plot the data correctly. Because there is no way to tell ggplot to create a histogram that can cross zero, we have to manually bin the data in order for data that crosses zero to be in the same bin. This won't shift the data on the axis, or remove data (as ggplot would).

```{r b-o binning function}
#### --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
##### Function to count decimal places #####
decimalplaces <- function(x) {
  if (abs(x - round(x)) > .Machine$double.eps^0.5) {
    nchar(strsplit(sub('0+$', '', as.character(x)), ".", fixed = TRUE)[[1]][[2]])
  } else {
    return(0)
  }
}

##### Function for binning when plotting circular histogram #####
circular.bins <- function(v, binwidth = NULL){
  decimals <- max(sapply(v, decimalplaces))
  bounds.zero <- c(360 - binwidth/2, 0 + binwidth/2)
  # bounds.zero <- round(bounds.zero, decimals)
  center.zero <- seq(round(bounds.zero[1], decimals), 360, by = 1/10^decimals)
  center.zero <- center.zero[-length(center.zero)] # remove 360
  center.zero <- append(center.zero, seq(0, bounds.zero[2], by = 1/10^decimals))
  bins <- seq(bounds.zero[2], bounds.zero[1], binwidth)
  cat <- NA
  for(b in 1:(length(bins) - 1)){
    ix <- which(between(v, bins[b], bins[b+1]))
    cat[ix] <- b
  }
  ix2 <- which(v %in% center.zero)
  cat[ix2] <- 0
  return(cat)
}
#### --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

Now that we have the function, we can create circular histograms with binwidth of 22.5, which is 360/16.

# Circular statistics

```{r stats data}
#### DATA ####
orientation <- fread("./Data/BurialOrientation.csv", na.strings = "")
```

## Test: circular statistics with burial sides

### Mean and variance

```{r stats test}
#### CIRCULAR MEAN AND VARIANCE ####
## Separate data based on burial side
left <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_left"][BurialSide_left == 1]
left[, BurialSide := "Left"]
right <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_right"][BurialSide_right == 1]
right[, BurialSide := "Right"]
back <- orientation[, .(Num, BurialOrientationMean, BurialOrientationMin, BurialOrientationMax), by = "BurialSide_back"][BurialSide_back == 1]
back[, BurialSide := "Back"]

# Bind together in a new table
sides <- rbind(left[, -1], right[, -1], back[, -1])

# Example data in degrees
sides <- sides[!is.na(BurialOrientationMean)]
left_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Left", BurialOrientationMean]
right_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Right", BurialOrientationMean]
back_angles <- sides[BurialSide == "Back", BurialOrientationMean]

# Convert to circular objects
left_circ <- circular(left_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock")
right_circ <- circular(right_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock")
back_circ <- circular(back_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock")

# Mean direction
mean_left <- mean.circular(left_circ)
mean_right <- mean.circular(right_circ)
mean_back <- mean.circular(back_circ)

# Variance direction
var_left <- var.circular(left_circ)
var_right <- var.circular(right_circ)
var_back <- var.circular(back_circ)

# Resultant length (measure of concentration)
rho_left <- rho.circular(left_circ)
rho_right <- rho.circular(right_circ)
rho_back <- rho.circular(back_circ)

## Table
stats <- data.table(Mean = c(mean_left, mean_right, mean_back),
                    Variance = c(var_left, var_right, var_back),
                    Rho = c(rho_left, rho_right, rho_back),
                    Side = c("Left", "Right", "Back"))
stats
```

### Angular distance

Here we create a function to calculate the distance between two angles, taking into account that angles can cross zero.

```{r stats angdist}
# Function to calculate smallest angular distance
angular_distance <- function(a, b) {
  diff <- abs(a - b) %% 360
  return(min(diff, 360 - diff))
}
# Example
angular_distance(350, 10)
angular_distance(190, 0)

# Calculate distances
dist_left_right <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_left), as.numeric(mean_right))
dist_left_back <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_left), as.numeric(mean_back))
dist_right_back <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_right), as.numeric(mean_back))

print(dist_left_right)
print(dist_left_back)
print(dist_right_back)
```

### Visualization

```{r stats viz}
## Circular means
sides_means <- c(mean_left, mean_right, mean_back)
names(sides_means) <- c("Left", "Right", "Back")
d <- list()
for(a in 1:length(sides_means)){
  d[[a]] <- sapply(1:length(sides_means), function(x){
    angular_distance(sides_means[a], sides_means[x])
  })
}
sides_mat <- do.call(cbind, d)
colnames(sides_mat) <- rownames(sides_mat) <- names(sides_means)
sides_mat[lower.tri(sides_mat)] <- NA
sides_dists <- melt(sides_mat)

# Plot burial orientations per country
sides_means_dt <- data.table(Sides = names(sides_means), Mean = sides_means)
sides_means_dt[, Mean := ifelse(Mean < 0, Mean + 360, Mean)]
ggplot(data = sides, aes(x = BurialSide, y = BurialOrientationMean, fill = BurialSide)) +
  geom_violin(width = 1, drop = F) +
  geom_point(data = sides_means_dt, aes(x = Sides, y = Mean), size = 2, shape = 23, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pals::brewer.set2(3)) +
  ylab("Burial orientation") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# Plot pairwise angular distances
ggplot(data = sides_dists[!is.na(sides_dists$value),]) +
  geom_tile(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = value), color = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradientn("Angular distance", colours = rev(pals::brewer.rdylbu(100)), 
                       na.value = "transparent",
                       limits = c(0,180)) + # maximum distance between angles?
                       # guide = guide_colorbar(barwidth = 1, barheight = 15)) +
  geom_text(aes(Var1, Var2, label = round(value, 1)), size = 10, size.unit = "pt") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Pairwise distance between angles means") +
  coord_equal(expand = F) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 0),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

### P-value

Now we shuffle the values of angles for each category and compute the differences in circular means and do a histogram where we plot the differences in circular means against the true difference. Do it for each of the three pairs. Make sure that each group has the same amount of observations.

```{r stats pval}
n <- min(c(length(left_circ), length(right_circ), length(back_circ)))

diffs <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){
  l <- sample(left_circ, n)
  r <- sample(right_circ, n)
  b <- sample(back_circ, n)
  mean_l <- mean.circular(l)
  mean_r <- mean.circular(r)
  mean_b <- mean.circular(b)
  dist_lr <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_l), as.numeric(mean_r))
  dist_lb <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_l), as.numeric(mean_b))
  dist_br <- angular_distance(as.numeric(mean_b), as.numeric(mean_r))
  return(list(dist_lr, dist_lb, dist_br))
})

diffs_lr <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 1))
diffs_lb <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 2))
diffs_br <- unlist(sapply(diffs, "[", 3))
diffs <- list(diffs_lr, diffs_lb, diffs_br)

## Plot histograms
hist(diffs_lr, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between left and right orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_left_right, col= "red", lwd = 3)

hist(diffs_lb, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between left and back orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_left_back, col= "red", lwd = 3)

hist(diffs_br, breaks = 100, main = "Difference between back and right orientations", xlab = "Angular distance"); abline(v = dist_right_back, col= "red", lwd = 3)

## Calculate p-value
# P = (X + 1) / (N + 1)
obs <- list(dist_left_right, dist_left_back, dist_right_back)
pval <- lapply(1:length(diffs), function(x){
  X <- sum(abs(diffs[[x]]) >= abs(obs[[x]]))
  N <- length(diffs[[x]])
  return((X + 1) / (N + 1))
})
names(pval) <- c("left_right", "left_back", "back_right")
pval
```

### Similarity

We can also calculate a similarity index that takes into account the distance between the means of the different categories.

```{r stats similarity}
# Similarity index
similarity_index <- function(d) {
  return(1 - (d / 180))
}

sim_left_right <- similarity_index(dist_left_right)
sim_left_back <- similarity_index(dist_left_back)
sim_right_back <- similarity_index(dist_right_back)

print(sim_left_right)
print(sim_left_back)
print(sim_right_back)
```

### Watson-William test and circular ANOVA

```{r stats anova}
## Watson-Williams test
# Combine data
all_angles <- c(left_angles, right_angles, back_angles) #right_angles, 
group <- factor(c(rep("left", length(left_angles)),
                  rep("right", length(right_angles)),
                  rep("back", length(back_angles))))

## Mardia-Watson-Wheeler test (non-parametric)
mww_result1 <- watson.two.test(left_circ, right_circ)  # pairwise example
mww_result2 <- watson.two.test(left_circ, back_circ)
mww_result3 <- watson.two.test(right_circ, back_circ)
print(mww_result1)
print(mww_result2)
print(mww_result3)

## Watson-Williams test
watson.williams.test(circular(all_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock"), group)

## Circular ANOVA 
aov.circular(circular(all_angles, units = "degrees", type = "angles", rotation = "clock"), group)
```

Now that we have tested different statistics using the left, right, and back angles, we can do the same for other categories, like periods, cultures, and countries.

### Difference between Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures

Here we are going to statistically test for differences in the orientations of Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures.

First of all, we look at the summary statistics for the two cultures. We can see that the means (mu) are quite different but the Corded Ware orientations are spread across the whole circle (there is very low concentration). This can be seen both by the rho value (mean resultant length) that is close to 0, and by the variance (var) value that is close to 1 ($var = 1 - rho$). The standard deviation runs from 0 to infinity, where higher values indicate a larger dispersion.

We can now try and check for differences in mean direction and concentration compared to a uniform distribution.

```{r stats cw-bb}
## Orientations
cordedware <- culture[["Corded Ware/Single Grave/Battle Axe/Fatyanovo"]]$BurialOrientationMean
cordedware <- circular(cordedware,
                      type = "angles",
                      units = "degrees",
                      rotation = "clock")

bellbeaker <- culture[["Bell Beaker complex"]]$BurialOrientationMean
bellbeaker <- circular(bellbeaker,
                      type = "angles",
                      units = "degrees",
                      rotation = "clock")

## Summary statistics of the two cultures
summary.dat <- data.frame(culture = c("Corded Ware", "Bell Beaker"),
                          mu = c(mean.circular(cordedware),
                                 mean.circular(bellbeaker)),
                          rho = c(rho.circular(cordedware),
                                  rho.circular(bellbeaker)),
                          var = c(var.circular(cordedware),
                                  var.circular(bellbeaker)),
                          sd = c(sd.circular(cordedware),
                                 sd.circular(bellbeaker)))
summary.dat

## Calculate mean direction and concentration from uniform distribution
cw_unif <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){
  r <- rcircularuniform(n = length(cordedware),
                            control.circular = list(
                              units = "degrees",
                              rotation = "clock"))
  m <- mean.circular(r)
  k <- rho.circular(r)
  return(list(m, k))
})
  
bb_unif <- lapply(1:1000, function(x){
  r <- rcircularuniform(n = length(bellbeaker),
                            control.circular = list(
                              units = "degrees",
                              rotation = "clock"))
  m <- mean.circular(r)
  k <- rho.circular(r)
  return(list(m, k))
})

cw_means <- sapply(cw_unif, "[", 1)
cw_rho <- sapply(cw_unif, "[", 2)

bb_means <- sapply(bb_unif, "[", 1)
bb_rho <- sapply(bb_unif, "[", 2)

hist(as.numeric(cw_means), breaks = 100, main = "Corded Ware", xlab = "Mean direction (mu)"); abline(v = mean.circular(cordedware), col = "red")
hist(as.numeric(cw_rho), breaks = 100, main = "Corded Ware", xlab = "Concentration (rho)", xlim = c(0,1)); abline(v = rho.circular(cordedware), col = "red")

hist(as.numeric(bb_means), breaks = 100, main = "Bell Beaker", xlab = "Mean direction (mu)"); abline(v = mean.circular(bellbeaker), col = "red")
hist(as.numeric(bb_rho), breaks = 100, main = "Bell Beaker", xlab = "Concentration (rho)", xlim = c(0,1)); abline(v = rho.circular(bellbeaker), col = "red")

# Similarity index (without folding over the horizontal axis)
obs <- culture_dists[Var2 == "Corded Ware/Single Grave/Battle Axe/Fatyanovo" & Var1 == "Bell Beaker complex"]$value
diff <- similarity_index(obs)
diff
paste0((1-round(diff,2))*100, "% different")
```

Now for modelling the differences between the two cultures, we can try using the `bpnreg` R package. This package performs a Bayesian circular regression model based on the projected normal distribution. The angles must be in radians. This is equivalent to an ANOVA.

In this model, the Bell Beaker is the reference culture. Thus, the value of the intercept for the categorical variables represents the mean of the Bell Beaker orientation.

Further reading:

-   <https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02040/full>

-   <https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/bmsp.12108>

-   <https://dspace.library.uu.nl/bitstream/handle/1874/361637/1_s2.0_S0022249616300827_main.pdf?sequence=1>

```{r stats cw-bb bpnreg, results='hide'}
# Data for regression
circ.dat <- data.frame(Angles = c(as.numeric(cordedware)*pi/180,
                                  as.numeric(bellbeaker)*pi/180),
                       Culture = c(rep("Corded Ware", length(cordedware)),
                                   rep("Bell Beaker", length(bellbeaker))))
circ.dat$Culture <- as.factor(circ.dat$Culture)

fit <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Culture, data = circ.dat, 
            its = 10000, burn = 100, n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```

```{r stats cw-bb bpnreg2}
# Means
aov.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit, "categorical", "radians")$Means))
aov.dt[, Culture := as.factor(c("Bell Beaker", "Corded Ware"))]

# Plot
plot.circular(c(aov.dt$LB[1], aov.dt$UB[1]), pch = 16, 
              rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(c(aov.dt$LB[2], aov.dt$UB[2]), pch = 5, 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(aov.dt$mean[1], pch = 16, col = "red", 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(aov.dt$mean[2], pch = 18, col = "blue", 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)

aov.dt[, .(Culture, deg(.SD)), .SDcols = c("mean", "mode", "sd", "LB", "UB")]

# Differences
diff.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences))
diff.dt[, Difference := "Bell Beaker/Corded Ware"]
diff.dt[, .(Difference, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)]

# Calculate angular distance between means
angular_distance(aov.dt$mean[1]*180/pi, aov.dt$mean[2]*180/pi)
```

In theory the HPDs of the two cultures overlap so the difference in means shouldn't be significant. When plotting the results, we can see that the two means are quite different and the HPDs overlap only because the spread of the Corded Ware orientations is extremely large. If we look at the differences table, the LB and UP of the HPD for the difference doesn't cross zero, so the difference between the two cultures is significant.

We can also try these other two tests that according to this paper seem to perform well with circular data, without falling too much into Type-1 and Type-2 errors.

<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-99299-5>

```{r stats watson.two}
## Watson's U2 test
watson.two(cordedware, bellbeaker)
```

So when the Watson's U^2^ test has a small p-value or a large test statistic, it means that the two groups are **NOT** homogeneious, so they are significantly different.

### Difference between Lažňany and Únětice cultures

Now let's double check that this interpretation is correct by comparing two other very similar cultures, e.g., Lažňany and Únětice. Únětice has a larger spread than Lažňany, but the means have a similar direction.

```{r stats lz-un bpnreg}
laznany <- circular(culture[["Lažňany"]]$BurialOrientationMean,
                    type = "angles",
                    units = "degrees",
                    rotation = "clock")
unetice <- circular(culture[["Únětice"]]$BurialOrientationMean,
                    type = "angles",
                    units = "degrees",
                    rotation = "clock")

summary.dat2 <- data.frame(culture = c("Lažňany", "Únětice"),
                          mu = c(mean.circular(laznany),
                                 mean.circular(unetice)),
                          rho = c(rho.circular(laznany),
                                  rho.circular(unetice)),
                          var = c(var.circular(laznany),
                                  var.circular(unetice)),
                          sd = c(sd.circular(laznany),
                                 sd.circular(unetice)))
summary.dat2
```

```{r stats lz-un bpnreg2, results = 'hide'}
# Data for regression
circ.dat2 <- data.frame(Angles = c(as.numeric(laznany)*pi/180,
                                  as.numeric(unetice)*pi/180),
                       Culture = c(rep("Lažňany", length(laznany)),
                                   rep("Únětice", length(unetice))))
circ.dat2$Culture <- as.factor(circ.dat2$Culture)

fit2 <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Culture, data = circ.dat2, 
            its = 10000, burn = 100, n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```

```{r stats lz-un bpnreg3}
# Means
aov.dt2 <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit2, "categorical", "radians")$Means))
aov.dt2[, Culture := as.factor(c("Lažňany", "Únětice"))]

# Plot
plot.circular(c(aov.dt2$LB[1], aov.dt2$UB[1]), pch = 16, 
              rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(c(aov.dt2$LB[2], aov.dt2$UB[2]), pch = 5, 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(aov.dt2$mean[1], pch = 16, col = "red", 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)
points.circular(aov.dt2$mean[2], pch = 18, col = "blue", 
                rotation = "clock", zero = pi/2)

aov.dt2[, .(Culture, deg(.SD)), .SDcols = c("mean", "mode", "sd", "LB", "UB")]

# Differences
diff.dt2 <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit2, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences))
diff.dt2[, Difference := "Lažňany/Únětice"]
diff.dt2[, .(Difference, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)]

# Calculate distance between means
angular_distance(aov.dt2$mean[1]*180/pi, aov.dt2$mean[2]*180/pi)

## Watson's U2 test
watson.two(laznany, unetice)
```

In this case we can see that the HPDs for the two cultures completely overlap and their means differ by only \~3 degrees. Furthermore, the LB and UB of the HPD for the difference crosses 0. Therefore, they are not significantly different from one another.

The Watson's U^2^ test also confirms this interpretation, as the p-value is greater than 0.10 and the test statistic is small.

### Difference across all cultures

For testing difference across all cultures (groups) we have to rotate the reference culture against which the regression is made. This is because the Intercept in these models is actually the reference culture, so each posterior summary statistic has to be interpreted against the group of reference.

Therefore, to look at the differences table we will have to fit a different model where the reference culture rotates.

But first, we can look at the means table which will always stay the same.

```{r stats cultures all, echo=TRUE, eval=T, results = "hide"}
culture <- split(orientation[Culture %in% culture_keep]
                 [, .(BurialOrientationMean, Culture, Longitude, Latitude, Age)], 
                 by = "Culture")
culture_means <- lapply(culture, function(x){
  mean.circular(circular(x$BurialOrientationMean, 
                         units = "degrees", 
                         type = "angles", 
                         rotation = "clock"),
                na.rm = T)
})
circ.dat.all <- lapply(culture, function(x){
  x$BurialOrientationMean <- x$BurialOrientationMean*pi/180
  return(x)
})
circ.dat.all <- rbindlist(circ.dat.all)
circ.dat.all$Culture <- factor(circ.dat.all$Culture, 
                               labels = c("Linearbandkeramik",
                                          "Lažňany",
                                          "Sopot",
                                          "Bell Beaker",
                                          "Únětice",
                                          "Corded Ware",
                                          "Baden",
                                          "Dnieper-Donets",
                                          "Trichterbecher",
                                          "Baltic Meso-Neolithic"),
                               levels = unique(circ.dat.all$Culture))

# Remove individual without Age
circ.dat.all <- circ.dat.all[!is.na(Age)]

# Model
fit.all <- bpnr(BurialOrientationMean ~ 1 + Culture, 
                data = circ.dat.all, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)

# Model fit
fit(fit.all)
```

The table shows the HPD of the means for each group. If the HPDs overlap across groups, the difference between those groups is not significant.

```{r stats cultures all2}
# Means
aov.dt.all <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit.all, "categorical", "radians")$Means))[1:10,]
aov.dt.all[, Culture := unique(circ.dat.all$Culture)]
# c1 <- sapply(strsplit(aov.dt.all$Culture, "Culture"), "[", 2)
# c2 <- sapply(strsplit(aov.dt.all$Culture, "Culture"), "[", 3)
# c1[is.na(c1)] <- c2[is.na(c2)] <- "Linearbandkeramik"
# aov.dt.all[, Culture := paste0(c1, "/", c2)]
aov.dt.all[, .(Culture, deg(.SD)), .SDcols = c("mean", "mode", "sd", "LB", "UB")]
```

```{r stats cultures all3, echo = FALSE, fig.dim=c(15,15)}
## Visualization with circlize package
```

The plot shows the posterior mean direction and HPD range of each culture. If the mean is outside the ranges of another culture, the difference between those cultures is significant.

We will test this statistically by fitting models with rotating group of reference.

```{r stats differences, results = "hide"}
# Rotate values so that reference culture is always a new one
culture.labels <- as.character(unique(aov.dt.all$Culture))
culture.labels <- lapply(0:(length(culture.labels)-1), function(i) {
  c(culture.labels[(i+1):length(culture.labels)], culture.labels[1:i])
})
culture.labels[[1]] <- culture.labels[[1]][1:10]

# Regression model list
differences.all <- lapply(culture.labels, function(l){
  # data
  circ.dat.all$Culture <- as.character(circ.dat.all$Culture)
  circ.dat.all$Culture <- factor(circ.dat.all$Culture, 
                                 levels = l)
  # model
  fit.m <- bpnr(BurialOrientationMean ~ 1 + Culture, 
                data = circ.dat.all, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
  # differences
  diff.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit.m, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)[1:9,])
  diff.dt[, Comparison := rownames(coef_circ(fit.m, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)[1:9]]
  c1 <- sapply(strsplit(diff.dt$Comparison, "Culture"), "[", 2)
  c2 <- sapply(strsplit(diff.dt$Comparison, "Culture"), "[", 3)
  c2[is.na(c2)] <- l[1]
  diff.dt[, Comparison := paste0(c2, "/", c1)]
  diff.dt[, .(Comparison, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)]
  diff.dt[, Overlapping := ifelse(between(0, LB, UB) | LB > UB, "No", "Yes")]
  return(diff.dt)
})
```

```{r stats differences2}
# Remove duplicated comparisons
dt <- rbindlist(differences.all)
dt$Comparison <- sapply(strsplit(dt$Comparison, "/"), function(pair) {
  paste(gtools::mixedsort(pair), collapse = "/")
})
dt <- dt[!duplicated(Comparison)][, .(Comparison, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB, Overlapping)]
dt[, Culture1 := sapply(strsplit(dt$Comparison, "/"), "[", 1)]
dt[, Culture2 := sapply(strsplit(dt$Comparison, "/"), "[", 2)]
dt <- dt[, .(Comparison, Culture1, Culture2, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB, Overlapping)][order(Culture1)]

datatable(dt[order(Culture1)][, .(Culture1, Culture2, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB, Overlapping, Comparison)], options = list(scrollX = TRUE))
```

#### Model with culture, space, and time

Here we are going to add latitude, longitude and age of the burial to the model. We want to test whether culture is indeed important for explaining patterns in burial orientation compared to just the location of the graves in space and time.

```{r stats cultures spatemp, echo=TRUE, eval=T, results = "hide"}
# Model
fit.sptemp <- bpnr(BurialOrientationMean ~ 1 + Culture + Longitude + Latitude + Age, 
                data = circ.dat.all, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```
```{r stats cultures spatemp2, echo=TRUE, eval=T}
fit.sptemp

# Model fit
fit(fit.sptemp)
```

In this case we can see that DIC and WAIC scores for the full model are smaller than the only culture one, meaning that culture added to space and time gives a better fit. 

#### Model with just space and time

Now we repeat by including only space and time, like in a baseline model.

```{r stats spatemp, echo=TRUE, eval=T, results = "hide"}
# Model
fit.sptemp.only <- bpnr(BurialOrientationMean ~ 1 + Longitude + Latitude + Age + Longitude:Latitude, 
                data = circ.dat.all, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```
```{r stats spatemp2, echo=TRUE, eval=T}
fit.sptemp.only

# Model fit
fit(fit.sptemp.only)
```

Based on the DIC and WAIC scores we can see that this model has the worst model fit across all three, with the full model being the most informative. This means that space and time are not enough to explain the patterns in burial orientation and therefore culture is a good predictor.

### Differences across cultures with orientations divided by body position

Here we are going to test for differences in cultures when dividing by body position. This means that for each position (left, right, back), we model the orientations against cultures.

#### Left

```{r stats cultures left, echo=TRUE, eval=T, results = "hide"}
# Add culture information to left data
left <- merge(left, orientation[, .(Num, Culture)], by = "Num", all.x = T)
nrow(left)
nrow(left[!is.na(Culture)][Culture %in% culture_keep])

# Remove NAs in Culture and keep only 10 most common cultures
culture_left <- left[!is.na(Culture)][Culture %in% culture_keep][, .(BurialOrientationMean, Culture)]

# Transform to radians
circ.dat.left <- culture_left
circ.dat.left[, Angles := BurialOrientationMean*pi/180]
circ.dat.left$Culture <- factor(circ.dat.left$Culture, 
                               labels = c("Linearbandkeramik",
                                          "Lažňany",
                                          "Sopot",
                                          "Bell Beaker",
                                          "Corded Ware",
                                          "Baden",
                                          "Dnieper-Donets",
                                          "Únětice",
                                          "Trichterbecher",
                                          "Baltic Meso-Neolithic"),
                               levels = unique(circ.dat.left$Culture))

# Model
fit.left <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Culture, 
                data = circ.dat.left, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```

```{r stats differences right, results = "hide"}
# Rotate values so that reference culture is always a new one
culture.labels <- as.character(unique(aov.dt.right$Culture))
culture.labels <- lapply(0:(length(culture.labels)-1), function(i) {
  c(culture.labels[(i+1):length(culture.labels)], culture.labels[1:i])
})
culture.labels[[1]] <- culture.labels[[1]][1:10]

# Regression model list
differences.right <- lapply(culture.labels, function(l){
  # data
  circ.dat.right$Culture <- as.character(circ.dat.right$Culture)
  circ.dat.right$Culture <- factor(circ.dat.right$Culture, 
                                 levels = l)
  # model
  fit.m <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Culture, 
                data = circ.dat.right, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
  # differences
  diff.dt.right <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit.m, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)[1:9,])
  diff.dt.right[, Difference := rownames(coef_circ(fit.m, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)[1:9]]
  c1 <- sapply(strsplit(diff.dt.right$Difference, "Culture"), "[", 2)
  c2 <- sapply(strsplit(diff.dt.right$Difference, "Culture"), "[", 3)
  c2[is.na(c2)] <- l[1]
  diff.dt.right[, Difference := paste0(c2, "/", c1)]
  diff.dt.right[, .(Difference, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)]
  diff.dt.right[, Significant := ifelse(between(0, LB, UB) | LB > UB, "No", "Yes")]
  return(diff.dt.right)
})
```

## Sex

```{r stats sex}
# Group sex
orientation[, Sex := ifelse(Sex < 0.5, 0, ifelse(Sex > 0.5, 1, Sex))]

## Circular means
sex <- split(orientation[, .(BurialOrientationMean, Sex = as.factor(Sex))], by = "Sex")
sex_means <- lapply(sex, function(x){
  mean.circular(circular(x$BurialOrientationMean, 
                         units = "degrees", 
                         type = "angles", 
                         rotation = "clock"))
})
sex_means <- unlist(sex_means)
sex_means <- sex_means[gtools::mixedsort(names(sex_means))]
d <- list()
for(a in 1:length(sex_means)){
  d[[a]] <- sapply(1:length(sex_means), function(x){
    angular_distance(sex_means[a], sex_means[x])
  })
}
sex_mat <- do.call(cbind, d)
colnames(sex_mat) <- rownames(sex_mat) <- paste0("Prob_", names(sex_means))
sex_mat[lower.tri(sex_mat)] <- NA
sex_mat
sex_dists <- reshape2::melt(sex_mat)

# Plot burial orientations per period
sex_means_dt <- data.table(Sex = names(sex_means), Mean = sex_means)
sex_means_dt[, Mean := ifelse(Mean < 0, Mean + 360, Mean)]

cols <- rev(pals::brewer.piyg(3))
cols[2] <- "grey80"

ggplot(data = orientation, 
       aes(x = as.factor(Sex), y = BurialOrientationMean, 
           fill = as.factor(Sex))) +
  geom_violin(width = 1, drop = F) +
  geom_point(data = sex_means_dt, aes(x = Sex, y = Mean), 
             size = 2, shape = 23, fill = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  ylab("Burial orientation") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.title.x = element_blank())

# Plot pairwise angular distances
ggplot(data = sex_dists[!is.na(sex_dists$value),]) +
  geom_tile(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = value), color = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradientn("Angular distance", colours = rev(pals::brewer.rdylbu(100)), 
                       na.value = "transparent",
                       limits = c(0, 180)) +
   geom_text(aes(Var1, Var2, label = round(value, 1)), 
            size = 10, size.unit = "pt") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Pairwise distance between angles means") +
  coord_equal(expand = F) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 0),
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

```{r stats sex bpnreg, results = "hide"}

sex.dt <- sex.dt[!is.na(Angles)]
sex.dt$Sex <- factor(sex.dt$Sex, levels = c("0", "0.5", "1"))

fit.sex <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + Sex, data = sex.dt, 
            its = 10000, burn = 100, n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```

```{r stats sex bpnreg2}
                x1 = sex.aov.dt$UB[1], y1 = ys[1],
                col = cols[1], lwd = 2)
circos.segments(x0 = sex.aov.dt$LB[2], y0 = ys[2], 
                x1 = sex.aov.dt$UB[2], y1 = ys[2],
                col = cols[2], lwd = 2)
circos.segments(x0 = sex.aov.dt$LB[3], y0 = ys[3], 
                x1 = sex.aov.dt$UB[3], y1 = ys[3],
                col = cols[3], lwd = 2)
circos.points(x = sex.aov.dt$mean[1], y = ys[1],
              bg = cols[1], pch = 21)
circos.points(x = sex.aov.dt$mean[2], y = ys[2],
              bg = cols[2], pch = 21)
circos.points(x = sex.aov.dt$mean[3], y = ys[3],
              bg = cols[3], pch = 21)
circos.clear()

# Differences
diff.dt <- setDT(data.frame(coef_circ(fit.sex, "categorical", units = "degrees")$Differences)[1:2,])
diff.dt[, Difference := c("0/0.5",
                          "0/1")]
diff.dt[, .(Difference, mean, mode, sd, LB, UB)]
```

It seems that 0 is different from 0.5 and 1. So we do see a difference between males and females, although this is of ~20 degrees. There is however no difference between females and the undetermined individuals.

## Circular linear regression models

For data that is not categorical (e.g., ancestry and mobility values), we have to use a regression model that is specific to angular data.

This regression models both the mean direction and the dispersion simultaneously. The model assumes that a circular response variable $\theta$ has a von Mises distribution with concentration parameter $\kappa$, and mean direction ($\mu$) related to a vector of linear predictor variables according to the relationship: $\mu + 2*atan(\beta*x)$, where $\mu$ and $\beta$ are unknown parameters, $\beta$ being a vector of regression coefficients, and $2*atan()$ being the link function.

The von Mises distribution is a function of $\mu$ and $\kappa$, where $\mu$ is the mean direction and $\kappa$ is the concentration parameter. A value $\kappa = 0$ corresponds to the circular uniform distribution; for $\kappa > 0$, the density is unimodal and symmetrical about $\mu$, and increasingly concentrated as $\kappa$ increases. For $\kappa \ge 2$ the density at the antipode $\mu + \pi$ is effectively zero, and the distribution is well approximated by a normal distribution with variance $1/\kappa$.

We can start with an initial value for $\beta$, to calculate $\mu$ and $\kappa$. These estimates can then be used to update the $\beta$ value, and then to update $\mu$ and $\kappa$, analogously to the ML equations for an independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) von Mises sample. This cycle is repeated until convergence. If $\beta = 0$, we have a null model where all observations cluster around a common mean direction $\mu$. However, as the elements of $\beta$ become infinite, the use of any monotone link function also leads to a null model with mean direction $\mu ± \pi$. In such cases, the likelihood will have a peak in the vicinity of zero, and attain a similar magnitude as the elements of $\beta$ tend to $± \infty$. **The optimization process is simplified if the x are centered at their means**.

**So should we scale our ancestry values?** (Whether we order the values or scale them, model results don't seem to change)

Further reads: <https://www.jstor.org/stable/2532334?seq=2>; <http://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1988/1/012108>

The `circular` package, has a `lm.circular` function that can be used for circular and linear data (c-l). We are going to test this function using the ancestry values associated to the grave individuals.

### CHG

```{r stats chg, fig.dim=c(10,10)}
y <- circular(rad(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$BurialOrientationMean), units = "radians", type = "angles", rotation = "clock")
x <- cbind(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$CHG, rep(1,length(orientation[!is.na(CHG)]$CHG)))
colnames(x) <- c("CHG", "Intercept")
mu <- as.numeric(mean.circular(y))
reg.chg <- lm.circular(y = y, x = x, type = "c-l", init = c(0,1))
reg.chg
```

We can see that CHG has a significant positive relationship with the mean direction of the burials. This test was made by using all the data as is. But what if we repeat the analysis by averaging the CHG value of the individuals that have the same burial orientation? Similarly to what we did to plot them.

```{r stats chg2}
## Based on average value across individuals with the same angle
dim_chg <- orientation[, mean(CHG, na.rm = T), by = c("BurialOrientationMean_sin", "BurialOrientationMean_cos")]
dim_chg <- dim_chg[!is.nan(V1),]
names(dim_chg)[3] <- "CHG"
# Get the angle from sin and cos (in radians)
dim_chg[, BurialOrientationMean := sapply(1:nrow(dim_chg), function(x) atan2(BurialOrientationMean_sin[x], BurialOrientationMean_cos[x]))]

# New variables for the linear regression model
y2 <- circular(dim_chg$BurialOrientationMean, units = "radians", type = "angles", rotation = "clock")
x2 <- cbind(dim_chg$CHG, rep(1, nrow(dim_chg)))
colnames(x2) <- c("CHG", "Intercept")
mu <- as.numeric(mean.circular(y2))
m <- mean(x2[,1])

# Model
reg.chg2 <- lm.circular(y = y2, x = x2, type = "c-l", init = c(0,1))
reg.chg2

# Plot
mu.df <- data.frame(mu = c(mu, reg.chg2$mu), type = c("Observed", "Estimated"))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dim_chg,
             aes(BurialOrientationMean_sin, BurialOrientationMean_cos, fill = CHG),
             shape = 21,
             size = 5,
             ) +
  geom_point(data = mu.df, aes(sin(mu), cos(mu), shape = type), size = 8) +
  scale_fill_gradientn("CHG", colors = pals::parula(100)) +
  scale_shape_manual(expression(mu), values = c(7, 8)) +
  xlab(expression(sin(theta))) +
  ylab(expression(cos(theta))) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 16))
```

## Bayesian circular regression with continuous data in `bpnreg`

We can also try using the same Bayesian regression model that we used for the categories.

For the continuous variable CHG we get a set of parameters, *bc*, *SAM* and *AS*, describing its effect on the circle. The coefficient *bc* represents the slope of the circular regression line at the inflection point. However, this may not be a representative effect for each dataset as the inflection point can lie in the extremes of the data or even completely outside the range of the predictor x. Therefore, two additional circular coefficients were developed by Cremers et al. (2018), the slope at the mean *SAM* and the average slope *AS.* The coefficient *SAM* represents the slope of the circular regression line at the average of the predictor and the coefficients *AS* represents the average slope over all values of x.

If the HPD intervals for all three circular coefficients (*bc, SAM and AS*) include 0, we do not find evidence that at the inflection point, at the average predictor value and on average the covariate influences the angular error.

<https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02040/full#B5> <https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bmsp.12108>

First I will center and scale all the ancestries together, so that the centering and scaling is not unique for each ancestry but it is based on all ancestry values together.

```{r stats bpnreg continuous, results = "hide"}
# Scale ancestries together so they are all on the same scale
ance <- orientation[, .(WHG, CHG, EHG, LVN)]
ance <- ance[!is.na(WHG)]
ance <- melt(ance)
ance$value <- scale(ance$value)

ance.dt <- orientation[, .(Angles = rad(BurialOrientationMean),
                          WHG, CHG, EHG, LVN, mobility)]
ance.dt <- ance.dt[!is.na(WHG)]
ance.dt$WHG <- ance[variable == "WHG"]$value
ance.dt$CHG <- ance[variable == "CHG"]$value
ance.dt$EHG <- ance[variable == "EHG"]$value
ance.dt$LVN <- ance[variable == "LVN"]$value
ance.dt <- ance.dt[!is.na(mobility)]
ance.dt$mobility <- scale(ance.dt$mobility)

fit.cont <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + WHG + CHG + EHG + LVN + mobility, data = ance.dt, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```

Based on the table for linear coefficients, it seems that all ancestries have an effect on the 2nd component (cosine) of the angles. Mobility does not seem to have an effect. Now to determine whether there is an effect on the circle, we have to look at the posterior HPDs of the circular coefficients, specifically bc, AS, SAM and SSDO. These will tell us if there is an accuracy or location effect.

```{r stats bpnreg continuous2}
fit.cont
```

When looking at the table, we can see that the HPDs for *bc* cross zero for all ancestries. This is also true for the HPDs for *SSDO*. If the HPD interval of the *SSDO* of a predictor does not include 0, the bivariate regression line does not run through the origin and therefore there is a location effect. Based on this and our HPDs for *SSDO*, we can conclude that **we do not have a location effect**. The effect that we see on the two components might therefore be an accuracy effect, an effect on the spread of the angles around the circles and not on the mean direction. *SAM* is the slope of the regression curve at the mean of the predictor data and the HPDs are outside zero for CHG, EHG and LVN. This means that at the average CHG, EHG, and LVN, with 1 unit increase we have an increase in the spread around the circle of 84.1˚, 54˚ and 33.8˚, respectively. When looking at the average slope at each predictor data point (*AS*), the HPD is outside zero only for CHG. This means that on average, a unit increase in CHG results in an increase of 86.5˚ in the spread around the circle.

We finish with a model that does not contain WHG.
```{r bpnreg no whg, results = "hide"}
fit.nowhg <- bpnr(Angles ~ 1 + CHG + EHG + LVN + mobility, data = ance.dt, its = 10000, burn = 1000, 
                n.lag = 3, seed = 1234)
```
```{r bpnreg no whg2}
fit.nowhg
```
